title: Show HN: Agents infer Lego mechanisms from sources, then animate them
author: antelocnova
summary: Hi there :) Around a month ago, I released LDraw Nova, an agentic toolset for assembling LEGO CAD models by generating LDraw source code files. For more details, here's the Show HN post: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49937916 From the comments, I got the impression that there was quite an interest in seeing not only AI-generated LEGO models, but also AI-animated LEGO ones. I took a look at results from past experiments, and found it feasible to use agentic LLMs for: - analyzing the LDraw source code for LEGO models - reverse-engineer! the mechanisms present by reading the descriptions and sequence for the parts there - and then, animate them via Blender! This new project I'm presenting, LDraw Mecha, is the end result and proof that can be done: - Read specially annotated LDraw LEGO models .mpd source files - Infer the model structure in terms of submodels - Select from those the ones that are mechanisms - Plan animations - Execute them in Blender In summary, from an initial .mpd source file, get a rigged and animated version for the model as a Blender (.blend) file. title: Get every new Xing job, with salaries, into a spreadsheet every morning
author: Ángel Panadero Rodríguez
summary: If you work with the German, Austrian or Swiss job market, whether in recruiting, HR tech, labour-market research or a job board, you have probably wanted Xing's job ads as data instead of web pages. Xing is the leading professional network in the DACH region, with around half a million active job postings at any time and thousands of new ones every day. In this post I show how to get them as clean JSON, CSV or Excel. That includes salary ranges, remote/hybrid information and career level, and a daily feed that only returns the jobs published since yesterday. You don't need to write a scraper: we'll use a ready-made one on Apify, called from Python. What you get for each job { "title" : "Python Developer Financial Services (all genders)" , "company" : "Exxeta" , "companySize" : "1.001-5.000 Mitarbeitende" , "city" : "Berlin" , "workplace" : "hybrid" , "employmentType" : "FULL_TIME" , "careerLevel" : "Mit Berufserfahrung" , "discipline" : "IT und Softwareentwicklung" , "language" : "de" , "salaryMin" : 59000 , "salaryMax" : 86000 , "salaryCurrency" : "EUR" , "salaryIsEstimate" : true , "datePosted" : "2026-09-17T05:36:36Z" , "applyUrl" : "https://career.exxeta.com/..." , "description" : "..." } Salaries are the interesting part. Many employers don't publish one, so Xing shows its own estimate instead. The data keeps them apart with salaryIsEstimate , so you can choose whether to trust estimates. 1. Get a token Create a free Apify account and copy your API token from Settings → API & Integrations . The free plan includes monthly credits, and the scraper costs $1 per 1,000 jobs, so testing is basically free. pip install apify-client export APIFY_TOKEN = "your-token" 2. Search by keyword and city import os from decimal import Decimal from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ " APIFY_TOKEN " ]) run = client . actor ( " angelrxdriguez/xing-jobs-scraper " ). call ( run_input = { " mode " : " search " , " keywords " : [ " python " ], " locations " : [ " Berlin " ], " maxItems " : 50 }, max_total_charge_usd = Decimal ( " 0.10 " ), # hard cap for this run ) dataset_id = run . default_dataset_id # run["defaultDatasetId"] on apify-client < 3 for job in client . dataset ( dataset_id ). iterate_items (): print ( job [ " title " ], " | " , job [ " company " ], " | " , job . get ( " workplace " ), " | " , job . get ( " salaryMax " )) Every keyword is searched in every city you list, and a single search can return more than 1,000 jobs. 3. Filter before you pay The filters run inside the scraper, so jobs that don't match are skipped and not charged. For example, English-language remote or hybrid jobs that pay at least €60k: run_input = { " mode " : " search " , " keywords " : [ " software engineer " , " data engineer " ], " locations " : [ " Berlin " , " München " , " Hamburg " ], " languages " : [ " en " ], " workplace " : [ " remote " , " hybrid " ], " minSalary " : 60000 , } If you're an English speaker looking for a job in Germany, that one query already saves you an evening of scrolling. 4. A daily feed of only the new jobs This is the mode I use the most. Instead of searching, feed mode reads Xing's public sitemaps, which list every active job, and onlyNewJobs remembers what you already received. Schedule it once a day and each run returns only the jobs published since the previous one: run_input = { " mode " : " feed " , " feedCities " : [ " Berlin " , " Hamburg " , " München " ], " feedKeywords " : [ " entwickler " , " developer " , " engineer " ], " onlyNewJobs " : True , " stateKey " : " my-daily-feed " , } The examples repo has a complete script that appends the new jobs to a CSV, ready for cron or Windows Task Scheduler. You can also skip code entirely: create a schedule in the Apify Console and connect the results to Google Sheets, Make or n8n. A note on doing this responsibly The scraper only uses pages that Xing's robots.txt allows for all crawlers. It collects job ads, not people's profiles, and it removes e-mail addresses and phone numbers from descriptions by default, so you don't end up storing recruiters' personal data. If you're in the EU, that matters for GDPR. Links Scraper: apify.com/angelrxdriguez/xing-jobs-scraper Examples in Python, Node.js and plain HTTP: github.com/angelrxdriguez/xing-jobs-api I built this scraper, so feedback is very welcome, especially on which fields or filters would make it more useful for you.

title: Cómo comprobar con Python que el texto censurado ha desaparecido de verdad de un PDF
author: Hanako H.
summary:
Un PDF censurado puede fallar de más maneras que «alguien dibujó un recuadro negro». El recuadro puede formar parte de la página o ser una anotación encima de ella, las marcas de censura pueden añadirse y no aplicarse nunca, la censura puede aplicarse y luego guardarse de forma incremental, de modo que la página antigua sigue dentro del archivo, y el nombre del autor puede estar todo el tiempo en los metadatos. En pantalla, todos estos casos se ven exactamente igual. Para ver cuáles filtran datos de verdad, generé siete versiones del mismo formulario de una página y revisé cada una con tres extractores de texto (PyMuPDF, pypdf y pdfminer.six), un escaneo de todos los streams del archivo y los metadatos. Una de las siete es el archivo guardado por el PDF Editor de la app de escritorio de osFoundry después de Find text and redact, Apply y Sanitize. Los scripts están al final; todo se ejecutó con Python 3.12, PyMuPDF 2.1, pypdf 6.21.4 y pdfminer.six 20260107 en un Apple M1. El formulario de prueba El formulario es una autorización de depósito directo generada con PyMuPDF (datos de ejemplo: nombre Jordan Ellis, número de cuenta 4471 2093 5568, teléfono (503) 555-0142). El número de cuenta aparece dos veces y el nombre también dos, y el campo de autor de la información del documento contiene el nombre. El texto usa la fuente Times integrada, así que cada línea del content stream es un simple TJ con los bytes escritos como cadena hexadecimal: BT 1 0 0 1 236 326 Tm /tiro 12.5 Tf [< 3434373120323039332035353638 >] TJ ET 34 34 37 31 20 32 30 39 33 ... es 4471 2093 ... en ASCII. Tenlo presente para la siguiente sección. Un recuadro dibujado no cambia nada en el texto La versión «censurada» que hace la mayoría de la gente dibuja rectángulos rellenos sobre los dos números de cuenta. En el content stream eso son dos objetos nuevos añadidos después de todo lo demás: q 232 322 89.25 17 re h 0 0 0 RG 0 0 0 rg B Q El TJ de arriba queda intacto. El rectángulo se pinta después, así que tapa los glifos en pantalla y en papel, pero todos los extractores leen los operadores de texto, no los píxeles. grep no sirve como prueba La comprobación obvia es buscar el número en el archivo: grep -c "4471 2093 5568" form.pdf # 0, for all seven files, including the original No devuelve nada ni siquiera para el original sin censurar, por dos motivos. Los content streams están comprimidos con Flate, así que los bytes en disco no son texto. Y aun después de descomprimirlos, el número está guardado como la cadena hexadecimal <3434373120...> , no como 4471 2093 5568 . Un escaneo de streams tiene que descomprimir cada stream y buscar las dos formas, que es lo que hace el comprobador de abajo. Con fuentes CID (la mayoría de los PDF en japonés, chino y coreano) ni siquiera eso funciona, porque la cadena contiene IDs de glifo que solo se traducen a caracteres a través de la tabla ToUnicode de la fuente. Un extractor de texto de verdad es la única comprobación que funciona en todos los casos; el escaneo de streams es una segunda línea para restos que los extractores no leen. Siete versiones, tres extractores Cada versión, comprobada buscando el número de cuenta. «Streams» cuenta los streams en cualquier parte de los bytes del archivo, en uso o huérfanos, que todavía lo contienen después de descomprimirlos: versión PyMuPDF pypdf pdfminer.six streams autor en los metadatos original encontrado encontrado encontrado 2 Jordan Ellis recuadro dibujado en la página encontrado encontrado encontrado 2 Jordan Ellis recuadro como anotación cuadrada encontrado encontrado encontrado 2 Jordan Ellis marcas de censura añadidas, sin aplicar encontrado encontrado encontrado 2 Jordan Ellis PyMuPDF apply_redactions , guardado completo – – – 0 Jordan Ellis PyMuPDF apply_redactions , saveIncr() – – – 2 Jordan Ellis osFoundry PDF Editor, Apply + Sanitize + Save – – – 0 (vacío) Para cualquier lector, las cuatro primeras son el mismo archivo. Los tres extractores coincidieron en todas las filas, así que para esta pregunta da igual cuál uses, siempre que uses alguno. La cuarta fila es la que pilla a quienes ya conocen las herramientas de censura. Censurar un PDF son dos pasos: una anotación Redact que marca una zona y un paso de aplicación que elimina lo que hay debajo. Un archivo guardado entre los dos muestra contornos rojos (o recuadros negros, según el visor) y sigue conteniéndolo todo. La trampa del guardado incremental La sexta fila pasa los tres extractores y aun así filtra datos. saveIncr() , igual que el Guardar normal de muchas herramientas PDF de escritorio, no reescribe el archivo. Añade los objetos modificados y una nueva tabla de referencias cruzadas después del %%EOF antiguo, y los lectores siguen la tabla más reciente. Los content streams antiguos siguen ahí, solo que ya nada los referencia. Recuperarlos cuesta una línea, porque la primera revisión del archivo termina en el primer %%EOF : raw = open ( " pymupdf-incremental.pdf " , " rb " ). read () first = raw [: raw . index ( b " %%EOF " ) + 5 ] print ( " 4471 2093 5568 " in pymupdf . open ( stream = first , filetype = " pdf " )[ 0 ]. get_text ()) # True El archivo incremental ocupa 11.533 bytes; sus primeros 7.163 bytes son el formulario original, intacto. Contar los marcadores %%EOF es una comprobación barata: el original y los guardados completos tienen uno, el guardado incremental tiene dos. Qué escribe en su lugar una eliminación real El archivo guardado por el PDF Editor de osFoundry no tiene el número de cuenta en ningún stream, y el resto del texto no se ha movido. Esta es la misma línea de antes, después de Apply: q BT 1 0 0 1 236 326 Tm /tiro 12.5 Tf [ -6500 ] TJ ET Q La cadena ha desaparecido y en el array de TJ solo queda un número. En un array de TJ , un número es un ajuste horizontal en milésimas del tamaño de fuente que se resta de la posición, así que -6500 mueve el cursor 6,5 × 12,5 = 81,25 puntos a la derecha sin dibujar nada. Es exactamente el ancho de 4471 2093 5568 en Times-Roman: texto eliminado tamaño de fuente ancho en Times-Roman valor en TJ Jordan Ellis 12,5 59,375 pt -4750 (503) 555-0142 12,5 78,11 pt -6249 4471 2093 5568 12,5 81,25 pt -6500 Jordan Ellis (firma) 15 71,25 pt -4750 Conservar el avance hace que todo lo que va después del fragmento eliminado en la misma línea se quede donde estaba. Comprobado palabra por palabra, las 63 palabras que quedan tienen la misma posición que en el original (0 movidas), y la página pasó de 75 palabras a 63. Los recuadros negros son un stream aparte al final, rectángulos rellenos sin más ( 236 323.5 81.25 12.5 re f ) del tamaño del texto eliminado, sin nada debajo. Los metadatos son un paso aparte El guardado completo de PyMuPDF eliminó el texto y dejó author = Jordan Ellis en la información del documento. La censura actúa sobre el contenido de la página, y el diccionario de información no es contenido de la página. Limpiarlo son dos llamadas: doc . set_metadata ({}) doc . del_xml_metadata () doc . save ( out , garbage = 4 , deflate = True ) En este formulario, eso deja vacíos todos los campos de información y ningún Jordan en ningún byte del archivo. El paso Sanitize document del editor hace lo mismo y además quita adjuntos, comentarios, campos de formulario, capas ocultas, marcadores y scripts, y su archivo guardado no tenía ningún metadato. Un comprobador para tener a mano Todo lo anterior en una sola función que devuelve una lista de problemas y sale con un código distinto de cero si hay alguno: import re , sys , zlib import pymupdf from pypdf import PdfReader from pdfminer.high_level import extract_text def problems ( path , secrets ): raw = open ( path , ' rb ' ). read () doc = pymupdf . open ( path ) flat = lambda t : re . sub ( r ' \s+ ' , ' ' , t . replace ( ' \xa0 ' , ' ' )) texts = { ' pymupdf ' : flat ( '' . join ( p . get_text () for p in doc )), ' pypdf ' : flat ( '' . join ( p . extract_text () for p in PdfReader ( path ). pages )), ' pdfminer ' : flat ( extract_text ( path )), } out = [] for s in secrets : out += [ f ' { name } : text contains { s !r} ' for name , t in texts . items () if s in t ] for p in doc : for a in p . annots (): if s in ( a . info . get ( ' content ' ) or '' ): out . append ( f ' annotation on page { p . number + 1 } contains { s !r} ' ) out += [ f ' metadata { k } = { v !r} ' for k , v in doc . metadata . items () if v and s in v ] if raw . count ( b ' %%EOF ' ) > 1 : out . append ( f ' { raw . count ( b " %%EOF " ) } revisions: earlier versions are still in the file ' ) if any ( p . first_annot and p . first_annot . type [ 1 ] == ' Redact ' for p in doc ): out . append ( ' redaction annotations were never applied ' ) for m in re . finditer ( rb ' stream?

Con el archivo del recuadro dibujado imprime 9 coincidencias de los extractores, el autor y cinco streams. Con el archivo del PDF Editor de osFoundry imprime clean . Tiene límites que conviene dejar claros. Solo encuentra las cadenas que le pasas, así que un valor escrito de otra forma ( 4471-2093-5568 ) necesita su propia entrada. Lee texto, así que un dato secreto que forma parte de una imagen necesita OCR primero. Y el escaneo de streams no ve el texto en fuentes CID, aunque los extractores sí lo detectan. El PDF Editor que generó el archivo limpio se ejecuta en local dentro de la app de escritorio, en línea con el diseño privado y local-first de osFoundry , así que el formulario no sale del equipo para censurarlo. La app es gratuita desde la página de descarga de osFoundry .

title: LLM Returns Invalid JSON Once in a While: Structured Outputs vs Validate-and-Retry
author: Libme
summary: TL;DR: If json.loads() on model output fails only occasionally, there are three distinct causes: truncation, stray prose or code fences around the JSON, and schema drift (valid JSON, wrong shape). Provider-side structured outputs (constrained decoding) eliminate the second and third for supported schemas; a validate-and-retry loop with a typed model covers everything else, including the first. In production you usually want both. What does the failure actually look like? The symptom that sends people to a search engine is usually one of these: json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0) json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Unterminated string starting at: line 1 column 140 (char 139) pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for Ticket priority Input should be less than or equal to 4 [type=less_than_equal, ...] They look alike but have different fixes: Symptom Real cause Right fix Expecting value: line 1 column 1 Model wrapped the JSON in a code fence or added "Here is the JSON:" Constrained decoding, or extract the outermost braces Unterminated string / Expecting ',' delimiter near the end Output hit max_tokens mid-object (truncation) Raise the limit, shrink the schema, check the stop reason Parses fine, then your code crashes on a missing key or odd enum value Schema drift: valid JSON, wrong shape Typed validation, or a strict schema on the provider side The first thing to do before changing any prompt: log the raw response and the stop/finish reason for every failure. Most "the model is flaky" reports I have seen turned out to be truncation, which no prompt wording can fix. Takeaway: classify the failure from the raw text and the stop reason before you touch the prompt. Step 1: Validate with a typed model instead of json.loads Parsing and validating in one step gives you an error message precise enough to feed back to the model. This uses Pydantic v2 and works with any provider, because call_model is just a function you supply. from typing import Callable , Literal from pydantic import BaseModel , Field class Ticket ( BaseModel ): category : Literal [ " bug " , " billing " , " feature_request " ] priority : int = Field ( ge = 1 , le = 4 ) summary : str = Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 200 ) def extract_json_object ( raw : str ) -> str : """ Strip code fences / chatter by taking the outermost braces. """ start , end = raw . find ( " { " ), raw . rfind ( " } " ) if start == - 1 or end <= start : raise ValueError ( " no JSON object found in response " ) return raw [ start : end + 1 ] def parse_ticket ( raw : str ) -> Ticket : return Ticket . model_validate_json ( extract_json_object ( raw )) The brace extraction is a blunt tool: it will not rescue truncated output, and it can mis-slice if the model emits two objects. That is fine, because the retry loop below catches those cases. Step 2: Retry with the error, not with the same prompt Resending the identical request is a coin flip. Sending the validation error back gives the model something concrete to correct. In Pydantic v2, ValidationError subclasses ValueError , so one except covers both parse and schema failures. Message = dict [ str , str ] def extract_ticket ( call_model : Callable [[ list [ Message ]], str ], prompt : str , max_attempts : int = 3 , ) -> Ticket : messages : list [ Message ] = [{ " role " : " user " , " content " : prompt }] last_error : ValueError | None = None for _ in range ( max_attempts ): raw = call_model ( messages ) try : return parse_ticket ( raw ) except ValueError as exc : last_error = exc messages += [ { " role " : " assistant " , " content " : raw }, { " role " : " user " , " content " : ( " That response failed validation: \n " f " { exc } \n " " Reply with only a corrected JSON object. " ), }, ] raise RuntimeError ( f " no valid output after { max_attempts } attempts " ) from last_error Two details that matter. Cap attempts at 2–3: each retry costs a full round trip and re-sends the growing conversation, so an uncapped loop turns one bad input into a bill spike. And if the failure was truncation, retrying with the same max_tokens will truncate again, so check the stop reason and raise the limit instead of looping. Takeaway: a retry that includes the exact validation error converges; a retry that repeats the prompt just re-rolls the dice. When do provider-side structured outputs replace the loop? Most major providers now offer some form of schema-constrained output: OpenAI's Structured Outputs with a strict JSON schema, tool/function calling with an input schema on Anthropic's API, and grammar- or schema-constrained decoding in local runtimes such as llama.cpp and in libraries like Outlines. The model's token choices are restricted so the output cannot violate the schema's syntax. As of late 2026 the details differ per provider, so check current docs for supported schema features. What this buys you: no code fences, no prose preamble, no invalid enum values, no missing required keys. If you want this without writing the plumbing yourself, OpenAI's Structured Outputs is the option that guarantees schema adherence on a strict schema, at the cost of being tied to that API. What it does not buy you: Truncation is still possible. If generation stops at the token limit, the object is still cut off. Strict mode does not make that safe. Only a schema subset is supported. Constraints like minLength , maximum , or deeply recursive structures are often unsupported or ignored, so your Field(ge=1, le=4) check may still need to run in your own code. Syntax is not semantics. A schema-valid priority: 4 can still be the wrong priority. Constrained decoding makes the shape certain, not the content correct. First-request latency. Some providers compile the schema on first use and cache it, so a rarely used schema can be slower on its first call. Takeaway: constrained decoding guarantees shape, not truncation-safety and not correctness, so keep your own validation behind it. Which approach should you use? Situation Use Hosted model, simple flat schema Provider structured outputs plus Pydantic validation Provider lacks strict mode, or schema uses unsupported constraints Validate-and-retry loop Local model (llama.cpp, Ollama-style runtimes) Grammar/schema-constrained decoding if your runtime supports it, retry loop as backstop Long outputs (big arrays, many records) Split into smaller calls; truncation risk grows with output length FAQ Why does the LLM return invalid JSON only sometimes? Sampling is probabilistic, so a model that follows your format 98% of the time will still occasionally add a code fence, stop mid-object at the token limit, or pick an off-schema value. Intermittent failures are normal without constrained decoding. Does asking for JSON in the prompt guarantee valid JSON? No. A prompt instruction raises the odds but guarantees nothing; only schema-constrained decoding restricts the output tokens, and even then truncation can break the object. How many retries should I allow for LLM JSON parsing? Two or three. If the third attempt still fails, the cause is usually truncation or an ambiguous schema, and more retries will not help. Bottom line If you call a hosted model with a simple schema, turn on the provider's strict structured output and keep a Pydantic model behind it for the constraints the schema cannot express. If you are on a provider or local model without it, the validate-and-retry loop above is enough for most small-team workloads. Either way, log the raw response and stop reason so you can tell truncation from drift. Cap retries, because the loop's failure mode is cost, not correctness. title: Persistent Vectorized Agent Memory: SQLite FTS5 to Cloud LibSQL
author: Satria Nindhita
summary: Persistent Vectorized Agent Memory: SQLite FTS5 to Cloud LibSQL Sebagian besar agen AI otonom yang beredar hari ini menderita amnesia selektif yang mahal. Arsitektur standar industri saat ini membengkak: mengarahkan tiap percakapan ke Pinecone atau Weaviate, membayar latensi jaringan 120ms per kueri RAG, lalu mengharapkan agen dapat mengeksekusi transaksi on-chain secara deterministik. Pola ini rapuh, lambat, dan membuang-buang modal komputasi. Jika Anda membangun sistem multi-agen yang mengelola likuiditas riil di Base L2, ketergantungan pada cluster vektor pihak ketiga adalah titik kegagalan infrastruktur ( single point of failure ). Solusi yang jauh lebih tahan uji adalah menyatukan memori leksikal, vektor embeddings, dan state transaksi langsung di mesin SQLite lokal menggunakan ekstensi FTS5, lalu mereplikasikannya ke edge melalui LibSQL (Turso). Mengapa Vektor Murni Menyesatkan Vektor semantik payah dalam mengenali string kriptografis presisi tinggi. Jika agen Anda bertugas memantau transaksi kas pada alamat 0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919 di Base (Chain ID 8453), model embedding seperti text-embedding-3-small sering kali mereduksi hash tersebut menjadi aproksimasi probabilitas. Ketika agen mencari: "Berapa gas yang dihabiskan 0x92Aff... pada transfer USDC kemarin?" , pencarian cosine similarity kerap mengembalikan alamat lain yang mirip secara leksikal di dalam ruang laten. Solusinya bukan memilih antara vektor atau leksikal, melainkan hybrid search deterministik di layer database embedded: SQLite FTS5 (BM25) untuk tokenisasi eksak: tx hash, chain IDs, fungsi ABI, dan public key. LibSQL Vector Search ( vector32 ) untuk abstraksi intent dan penalaran strategi trading. Arsitektur: Local In-Memory ke Cloud LibSQL Dengan LibSQL, memori agen ditulis secara lokal di NVMe instance (latensi sub-milidetik), lalu di- stream secara asinkron ke cluster global. Mesin agen tetap ringan, dapat mati dan hidup kembali tanpa kehilangan jejak memori. title: Both URLs followed main, so my residual could mix two dates
author: pm25coder
summary: A reader left a note under my last post that I have not been able to put down. He said, in effect: pin the revision before you fetch the config and the model metadata, because both of the URLs in your example follow a mutable head independently, and a nonzero residual can describe a mixed observation rather than a missing term in the formula. He is right, and it is not a theoretical race. The snippet he was reading asks two URLs: https://huggingface.co/{repo}/raw/main/config.json https://huggingface.co/api/models/{repo} Both follow main . Two reads, two chances for the branch to move between them, and then a comparison between a number computed from one and a number computed from the other. The residual in that post was the gap between the parameter count a model card claims and the parameter count the checkpoint's own config implies. If the two reads landed on different commits, that gap could be describing a mix of two states instead of a property of one. So this week I measured what it costs to stop doing that. Why the snippet has two URLs at all I did not fetch two URLs because I like two URLs. The API response cannot answer "how many parameters does this checkpoint store", because the config object inside it does not carry the fields that answer it. Across seven repos, api/models/{repo} returned a config object with three keys — architectures , model_type , tokenizer_config — and four for Phi-3-mini, which adds auto_map . None of the seven carried vocab_size , num_hidden_layers or hidden_size . Those three live in config.json , and I could not reach them from the metadata call. So the shape is forced: one call for what the API knows, one call for the file the API does not inline. The only open question is which revision the second call names. What the two paths returned today Seven repos, four model families, all ungated, read in one sitting: repo sha (first 12) safetensors.total main vs pinned HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct 12fd25f77366 134,515,008 same HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct a10cc1512eab 361,821,120 same HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct 31b70e2e869a 1,711,376,384 same Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct 7ae557604adf 494,032,768 same Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct 989aa7980e4c 1,543,714,304 same microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct f39ac1d28e92 3,821,079,552 same allenai/OLMo-1B-hf aee7752d9c08 1,176,764,416 same "Same" is not a shrug in that column. Both paths answered 200, both returned the same config values (I compared vocabulary size, layer count, hidden size, tie flag, dtype and architecture string), both returned the same byte count — 861, 846, 908, 659, 660, 967 and 632 — and both carried the same ETag header. Seven out of seven. That last part is what I did not expect, and it is exactly the trap. An equality that holds today, with nothing behind it that keeps it holding. The ETag earns you one true sentence: these two paths currently resolve to the same object. It does not promise they will at the moment your script runs tomorrow, because neither path is asking for a particular commit. Only the sha does that, for the plain reason that the sha is the request. What pinning costs, and a correction In the reply I sent that reader, I wrote that pinning the revision costs one extra request. Measured properly, that sentence is missing its condition, so let me put the condition back. If your script already calls api/models/{repo} — mine did, because it needed safetensors.total — then the sha arrives in that very response, sitting next to the total. Pinning then costs zero extra requests: the same two calls, with one of them naming a sha instead of main . The extra request only appears in the other case: a script whose only read is raw/main/config.json , because all it wants is the config. That one goes from one call to two. So the honest version is: zero if you were already asking the API for anything, one if you were not. I wrote down the second half as if it were the whole answer. Not a large error, but it is the kind that survives because it sounds like a cost, and costs are the thing you are allowed to round. The order that removes the ambiguity Three steps, and no new dependency: GET api/models/{repo} and keep sha — plus safetensors.total if your comparison needs it. GET raw/{sha}/config.json , and recompute what the checkpoint stores from the config you just pinned. Compare the two numbers. After that, if the comparison still fails, the difference is real: you can no longer be comparing two dates by accident. The change is one string in a URL. What it buys is that every number in your table belongs to the same commit, and that someone who re-runs your script next month gets the same artifact you described — or an error, which is also an answer. What I did not measure Whether any of these seven repos actually moved between two of my reads. I cannot replay the past, and the identical ETag s only say the paths agree now. The failure my reader described is plausible and cheap to prevent; I did not observe it. Gated repos. All seven I tried were ungated and answered 200. A gated repo may treat raw/{sha} differently from raw/main , and I do not know which way. The web UI's metadata. I read the API and the raw file, not the page. Whether main had moved at all since the post my reader was reading. That post is a day old; its own reads are not reproducible now, which is the whole point. Seven repos is not a survey. It is seven repos, named above, so you can run the same seven and check me.

title: Building a Client-Side Image Compressor: No Server, No Upload, Just JavaScript
author: Toolenix
summary: My most-used tool shrinks images without sending a single byte anywhere. Here's the 30 lines of JavaScript that do it. Every image compressor you've used uploads your photo to a server, compresses it there, and sends it back. That works — but it means your photos leave your device. I built the Image Compressor on Toolenix to do the whole job in the browser. No upload, no server, no waiting on a network. Here's how it works. The core idea: canvas does the work The browser's element can decode an image, redraw it at a smaller size, and export it as a compressed JPEG — all locally. That's the entire trick. Three steps: Read the file into an with URL.createObjectURL . Draw it onto a canvas at the target dimensions. Export with canvas.toBlob() at a quality setting you choose. The code Here's the heart of it — a function that takes a file and a target width, and returns a compressed blob: async function compressImage ( file , maxWidth = 1920 , quality = 0.8 ) { const img = await loadImage ( file ); // Keep the aspect ratio, shrink only if larger than maxWidth const scale = Math . min ( 1 , maxWidth / img . width ); const width = Math . round ( img . width * scale ); const height = Math . round ( img . height * scale ); const canvas = document . createElement ( ' canvas ' ); canvas . width = width ; canvas . height = height ; const ctx = canvas . getContext ( ' 2d ' ); ctx . drawImage ( img , 0 , 0 , width , height ); // toBlob with 'image/jpeg' + quality does the compression return new Promise (( resolve ) => { canvas . toBlob ( resolve , ' image/jpeg ' , quality ); }); } function loadImage ( file ) { return new Promise (( resolve , reject ) => { const img = new Image (); img . onload = () => resolve ( img ); img . onerror = reject ; img . src = URL . createObjectURL ( file ); }); } Quality 0.8 is the sweet spot in my experience: files shrink dramatically with no visible difference for web use. Drop to 0.6 for thumbnails, raise to 0.9 when quality matters more than size. The details that make it feel like a real tool The compression is the easy part. The UX around it is what makes people come back: Drag and drop — handle dragover / drop events, accept multiple files at once. Before/after sizes — show the original KB and the compressed KB side by side. People love seeing "2.4 MB → 380 KB". Batch download — loop over files, compress each, and offer a single ZIP or individual downloads. Memory hygiene — call URL.revokeObjectURL() after you're done, or a long session leaks memory with every image. Why client-side wins for tools like this Privacy: a photo never leaves the device. For personal photos, that's the feature. Speed: no upload time, no queue, no server round-trip. Compression of a typical photo takes well under a second. Cost: static hosting. No server to scale, no bandwidth bill for other people's photos. Reliability: nothing to go down. If the page loads, the tool works — even offline after the first load. The limits (honestly) Canvas compression isn't magic. It can't beat a dedicated encoder on every image, PNG transparency needs care (JPEG has no alpha channel — draw onto a white background first or keep PNG output), and very large images can still spike memory. For a free web tool, though, it's more than good enough. Try it The compressor is live at toolenix.com — free, no sign-up, and your images never leave your browser. The whole site is built on the same idea: 113 tools, all client-side.

title: Why I Built a Native Telegram Booking Mini App (Go + React) to Stop the "What Time Works for You?" DM Ping-Pong

title: Link Building Cost for Small Businesses
author: Veduis
summary: Link building cost for small businesses usually lands between $300 and $1,500 a month for DIY outreach, or $1,500 to $5,000 a month for a retainer agency that delivers three to eight links. Published rates run $150 to $600 for a niche blog placement and $2,000 or more for a single high-authority link. The cheapest option is not cheaper links. It is one linkable asset and one outreach motion, run by someone already on payroll. Below are real rates by tactic, what retainers actually deliver, and where the money gets wasted. Backlinks remain one of Google's strongest ranking signals. A page with more authoritative, relevant backlinks outranks a technically superior page with fewer. The challenge for small businesses is that link building is one of the most time-intensive SEO activities, and most of the common advice, "just create great content", isn't operationally specific enough to act on. This guide covers the tactics that produce actual links for businesses without a dedicated PR team or a $10,000/month agency budget. What Makes a Good Link Before acquiring links, understand what Google values: Domain authority: A link from the New York Times is worth hundreds of links from random blogs. Domain Rating (Ahrefs) and Domain Authority (Moz) are proxy metrics; use them as filters, not absolutes. If your on-page foundation is still shaky, run a technical SEO audit first. Links amplify a sound site; they cannot rescue a broken one. Relevance: A link from a site in your industry is more valuable than a link from an unrelated site, even if the authority is similar. A link to a plumbing business from a home improvement site beats a link from a gaming site. Anchor text: The clickable text of the link. "Click here" passes less context than "PostgreSQL performance tuning guide." You can't fully control this, but topically relevant anchor text matters. Link placement: Links in the main content body of an editorial article are more valuable than footer links, sidebar links, or links in sponsored directories. Follow vs. nofollow: rel="nofollow" links don't pass PageRank directly. Still valuable for traffic and brand signals, but less SEO impact than followed links. Strategy 1: Digital PR and Original Data The highest-ROI link building strategy for most businesses is creating content that journalists and bloggers want to cite. The same citation logic now drives visibility in AI answers, which our answer engine optimization guide covers in detail. Data-driven content works best: Original surveys of your customers or industry Annual benchmark reports Proprietary data analysis (if you have data from your SaaS product, anonymized) Novel research on a topic relevant to your industry Example: A payroll software company surveys 500 small businesses about remote work policies and publishes an annual report. HR blogs, business publications, and employment lawyers cite the statistics. Each citation is a backlink. Execution: Identify a question your target audience cares about that doesn't have current data Survey your email list, customers, or a panel service (Pollfish: $100-500 for 200 responses) Publish the findings as a dedicated report page (not a blog post) Outreach to journalists who cover your space with the data as a story angle Monitor who covers the story and follow up for links Strategy 2: Resource Page Link Building Resource pages are curated lists of helpful tools, guides, or links in a specific niche. If you have genuinely useful content, you can earn placement on these pages. Finding resource pages: Search Google with operators like "[keyword]" + "resources" , "[keyword]" + "useful links" , "[keyword]" + inurl:resources , and "[keyword]" + intitle:"resources" . For example: "email marketing" + "resources" or "small business accounting" + inurl:resources . Outreach template (brief, specific): Use a subject line like Resource suggestion for [Page Title] . Open by noting you found their page while researching their topic and that it is a solid list. Mention a similar resource they already link to, then describe your resource with its specific angle and why it fits their list. Drop your URL, and close by offering to mention their content to your audience in return. Response rates for resource page outreach are 5-15%, better than cold guest post pitches. The key is genuine relevance: don't pitch a list about plumbing for a digital marketing resource page. Strategy 3: Broken Link Building Find pages in your niche that link to resources that no longer exist (404 errors). Offer your content as a replacement. Use Ahrefs, Semrush, or the Check My Links Chrome extension for this. First, find resource pages in your niche using the same search operators as above. Second, run each page through the Ahrefs Broken Link Checker or Check My Links to surface dead outbound links. Third, identify broken links that your content could credibly replace. Finally, contact the site owner with the broken link and your replacement. A working subject line is Broken link on [Page Title] : point out that the link to "[Broken Link Text]" is returning a 404, offer your current guide covering the same topic with your URL, and offer to have them swap it in. This works because you're providing genuine value (fixing their page) alongside the request. Strategy 4: HARO and Journalist Outreach Help a Reporter Out (HARO) sends three daily emails with journalists requesting expert sources for articles. If your response is published, you typically get a byline with a link. Making HARO work: Reply within 1-2 hours of the email (slots fill fast) Be specific and quotable; journalists don't want vague opinions Keep responses under 200 words Include your credentials and why you're the right source Have a professional headshot and bio ready Example of the response shape that gets used: RE: Small business accounting software question Your Name, Owner at Your Company (yoursite.com): "The biggest accounting mistake small businesses make is waiting until tax time to reconcile. I recommend a weekly 20-minute reconciliation -- match every bank transaction to a record in your accounting software. This takes 15 minutes when you're current; it takes 15 hours when you're six months behind. For tools: QuickBooks for businesses with accountants already in that ecosystem, Xero for businesses that want better bank reconciliation and don't need the QuickBooks name recognition." Alternative: Use Qwoted , SourceBottle , or Featured for similar journalist sourcing opportunities with less competition than HARO. Free Link Building for Small Businesses: Citations and Listings For businesses with a local component, citations (mentions of your business name, address, and phone, NAP) on authoritative directories build local ranking authority. Priority citation sources: Google Business Profile (mandatory) Bing Places for Business Apple Maps Yelp Better Business Bureau Industry-specific directories (Avvo for lawyers, Healthgrades for medical, Houzz for contractors) Local Chamber of Commerce NAP consistency: Your business name, address, and phone number must be identical across all citations. Inconsistencies confuse Google's local ranking algorithm. The full platform-by-platform process lives in our local SEO optimization post . Start with the Google Business Profile setup sequence before you pay for citations at scale, because a wrong category poisons every listing downstream. Use BrightLocal ($29/month) to audit and manage local citations at scale. What to Avoid Paid links: Google explicitly prohibits buying links. Modern link schemes are sophisticated; if it feels like you're paying for placement, you probably are. The risk is a manual penalty that can collapse your organic traffic overnight, and the recovery path after a core or spam update is slow and rarely complete. Private Blog Networks (PBNs): Networks of fake sites that exist only to sell links. These work until they don't; Google's link spam updates have repeatedly deindexed PBNs in bulk. Mass guest posting for links: Guest posting on relevant, editorial sites is legitimate. Guest posting on low-quality sites solely for anchor text links is a spam tactic. Reciprocal link schemes: "I'll link to you if you link to me" at scale. Occasional natural reciprocal linking is fine; systematic link exchanges are a signal of manipulation. How Much Does Link Building Cost? Here is what each route costs in 2026, before you negotiate anything: Route Typical 2026 rate Cost per link DIY outreach, part-time $300 to $1,500 a month for 1 to 3 links $300 to $800 Freelance outreach help $25 to $60 an hour for 1 to 2 links a month $400 to $900 Resource page or broken link campaign $500 to $2,000 a month for 2 to 4 links $250 to $600 Retainer agency $1,500 to $5,000 a month for 3 to 8 links $400 to $1,200 Paid niche blog placement $150 to $600 each $150 to $600 Digital PR on original data $3,000 to $12,000 up front for 5 to 30 links if it lands $150 to $1,500 Major publication placement $2,000 or more each $2,000 and up Cost per link is the number to negotiate on, and it varies by tactic. Quotes I have collected for clients in 2026: freelance outreach help runs $25 to $60 an hour; a retainer agency asks $1,500 to $5,000 a month for three to eight links; paid placements on niche blogs run $150 to $600 per link; a digital PR campaign built on an original data asset costs $3,000 to $12,000 up front; and a single placement in a major publication can exceed $2,000. Divide monthly spend by new referring domains to get cost per link, then compare that against the revenue the acquired links produce. Track in Ahrefs or Semrush: Domain Rating / Domain Authority trend over time New referring domains per month Link quality distribution (filter by DR > 30 to see meaningful links) Organic traffic correlation with link acquisition Set realistic expectations: meaningful ranking impact from a link building campaign typically appears in 3-6 months. Links from a single domain have diminishing returns, diversity of referring domains matters more than volume from one source. The most sustainable link building strategy for a small business is producing content worth linking to (detailed guides, original data, free tools) and doing consistent outreach. Shortcuts exist but don't last. The businesses that maintain strong backlink profiles do so because they have genuinely linkable assets and systematically promote them. What Most Guides Get Wrong Most link building advice fails small businesses in the same handful of ways. Domain Rating as a target instead of a filter. It treats Domain Rating as the target rather than a filter: a local plumber chasing DR 70 links will waste months on outreach that a DR 35 regional publication would have answered in a week, because relevance and geography beat raw authority for local rankings. Tactic collection instead of repetition. It overvalues the number of tactics tried and undervalues repetition of one tactic, since a single resource page campaign run for six months consistently outperforms five strategies attempted for two weeks each, and response rates compound as your sender reputation and templates improve. No linkable asset to point at. It ignores the asset problem: most small business sites have nothing worth linking to, and no outreach template fixes that, so the honest sequence is build one linkable asset first, then run outreach against it for a full quarter before judging results. Speed beats eloquence in journalist requests. Most guides underreport how much of HARO success is speed rather than eloquence, because the businesses winning those links reply within the first hour with a competent answer, not a day later with a perfect one. No follow-up after the first citation. They also skip the follow-up: a journalist who cites your data once will usually cite your next report if you email them directly the day it publishes. Link building treated as an isolated activity. It gets presented as an isolated activity when it works best as a byproduct of being the most data-rich, most cited voice in a narrow niche, which is a positioning decision, not an SEO tactic. Conclusion Backlinks remain a decisive ranking signal, but small businesses win them with assets and repetition, not budgets. Build one genuinely linkable asset first, whether that is a data report, a free tool, or the most detailed guide in your niche. Then commit to one outreach motion for a full quarter, with resource page placements and broken link replacement as the best starting points. Track new referring domains instead of raw link counts, and keep your NAP consistent if you serve a local market. Skip paid links, PBNs, and mass guest posting, because a manual penalty erases more value than a year of shortcuts creates. Pair link work with a technical SEO audit so the authority you earn lands on a site Google can crawl and index cleanly. Start this week by sending five resource page outreach emails.

title: I ran 3 Claude Code architecture diagram tools on my repo. Here's what each one got right
author: Valentina Koniukhova
summary: My project, worklore , is a small app that grew in all directions: a Python backend on AWS Lambda, a plain-JS site, an MCP connector for agents, and four more repos around it. I wanted a picture of it I could trust. So in one day I ran three open-source tools that turn code into a diagram or a map, all three as plugins for Claude Code: Floorplan : a map of the app with its parts, endpoints and user flows. Archify : one architecture diagram, every box linked to the exact lines of code. Understand Anything : a knowledge graph of every file, function and class, with a guided tour. Floorplan's README has a nice table comparing the three. It says what each tool answers and who it's for. It has no time, no cost and no pictures of the other two. This post fills that in, on one real codebase, and then does the test I actually care about: can each one answer real questions about my own code? The short version Floorplan Archify Understand Anything What you get a map you can click through, with flows one diagram, boxes linked to code a graph of 732 nodes with a tour Time to first result a few minutes about an hour, with two failed runs and two card fixes 14 minutes Cost on my Claude plan, not measured separately on my Claude plan, not measured separately $13 at API prices (measured) Answers questions yes, an Ask bar no yes, a chat command What went wrong user flows written from memory, two of them wrong cards written from memory, one wrong twice nothing I could find Floorplan: the map is right, the flows were not Floorplan read my 166 files and drew them as parts with plain-words descriptions. The first surprise: it found 0 endpoints. My server keeps its routes in one table keyed by "METHOD /path" , not in a framework router. I opened a pull request to read that shape, and the author merged it 70 minutes later. Then it showed all 66. The real trap was the user flows. While building the map, the agent also wrote flows, and it wrote them from its memory of my app. One said a person can publish a story from the website. The site can't do that. Another got wrong how a story gets drafted for someone else. A wrong flow and a right one look the same on the map. What fixed it was a button Floorplan already has: Request a new flow . You describe a flow in plain words, and the agent traces it through the code, tying every step to a route or a function. I deleted the hand-written flows and requested 17. Then I ran 16 of them against a staging copy of my backend: 14 work, one partly, one can't be tested there. The 17th, a nightly job on my Mac, had been quietly failing for two nights. I wrote it up step by step, so your agent can redo it on your app: My agent drew my app's user flows from memory and got two wrong; Floorplan's traced ones were right . Archify: one diagram for five repos Archify draws from a JSON description and then checks it hard: every cited line must exist at the pinned commit, and the last check opens the diagram in a real browser. What its docs don't say up front: a diagram pins exactly one repository . My project lives in five, and the links between them aren't code at all. One repo is a skill that tells an agent to call my API with curl; another is a scanner my server keeps a copy of. A tool that follows imports sees five islands. So I pinned the repo where the system runs, linked its boxes to lines of code, and drew the other repos as named boxes with a card saying what each holds. Two runs failed first: my SSH remote was rejected for web links (the HTTPS form works), and my uncommitted edits shifted line numbers away from the committed bytes Archify checks against. Archify proves the cited lines exist. It does not prove what a card says. One of mine, "how stories get written", was wrong twice, again from my agent's memory. The full recipe: One architecture diagram for a project split across five repos, with Archify . Understand Anything: the most thorough, the most expensive I ran Understand Anything headless, so I got exact numbers: 14 minutes, 16 helper agents working in batches of five, and $13.01 at API list prices (on a Claude subscription it comes out of your plan instead). Its README warns that the first run uses a lot of tokens. It does. What you get is a lot: 732 nodes (files, functions, classes, config, docs), 1,625 links, 9 layers, and a 15-step tour that starts at the README and walks through the code in a sensible order. Every function has a one-line summary. I checked the summaries in the places where my agent had been wrong from memory, and they were right. Two things to know before installing it. Its start-of-session hook tells the agent to rebuild a stale graph and "Do not ask the user for confirmation" (only if you turn auto-update on). And its dashboard runs as a local server; in a headless run it died after 10 minutes, when Claude Code stops background jobs. It feels made for someone else's project: the tour and the summaries teach you a codebase you've never seen. The real test: three questions about my own code Pictures are nice. What I wanted was answers. I asked each tool the same three questions, the kind I'd ask before changing anything: How do we decide whether a person has enough rights for an action, in the MCP connector and in the REST API? What numbers do we keep about reproductions and other actions, including anonymous ones? What do we log, and where? Floorplan got them in its Ask bar, Understand Anything in its chat command, and for Archify an agent that could see only the diagram. Then a plain agent with no map at all read the code to make an answer key. Floorplan Understand Anything Archify No map, just code Time 61 s 91 s ($0.72) 33 s ($1.18) 166 s Rights right, short right, most detailed "reading is public, writing needs a token" complete Counters right, about half right, nearly complete almost nothing complete Logs right, short right, detailed one line complete Mistakes none none none, and it said what it didn't know — Nobody made anything up, which already beats my agent's memory. But look at how they got there. Floorplan's Ask reads the map and the code, by design. Understand Anything's chat is meant to answer from the graph, yet it opened the source files anyway and said so. Archify has no way to answer questions, and the diagram simply doesn't hold this level of detail. And the plain agent reading code found things none of the three did. The biggest was a security hole. When an AI app connects to worklore through OAuth, the sign-in advertised two permissions, worklore.read and worklore.write . The code never checked them. The app got an ordinary account pass, and that pass also worked on the site's REST API: it could delete my stories, change their visibility, and, since I'm the admin, open the admin pages. All three maps described the sign-in correctly, as a flow. None of them asked what the token could reach once issued, because that isn't a box or an arrow. I fixed it before publishing this. An app's pass is now marked as one, works only through the connector, and only within what you approved; an app that asks only to read can't write. A new test walks the whole OAuth flow and then tries the pass on every kind of route. The same agent found more places where my code and my own documents disagreed. My privacy page left out Google sign-in, described "standard server logs" with IPs that my application doesn't write (the CDN logs do, for 14 days), and called my analytics page-views-only when the server also sends events, some with the caller's IP, and the site sends the text of searches that find nothing. Smaller ones: a doc that says a log field holds a raw id when the code hashes it, a counter that also counts HEAD requests, agent reads over MCP that never count as reads, and staging logs that were kept forever (now 90 days, like production). I rewrote the privacy page against the code; the rest of the smaller ones are on my list. None of it is "architecture", so no map shows it. So which one should you use? You inherited a codebase, or you're about to contribute to someone else's: Understand Anything. The tour and the per-function summaries are the fastest way in, if the token bill is fine. You own a small app and want to know what users can actually do: Floorplan, but delete every flow it wrote while building the map and request them again, so each step is traced to code. Then test them. You need one picture for a README, a pitch or a new teammate: Archify. It's the only one whose output is a single, checked diagram you can share. Check the cards yourself. You need to know whether your code keeps your promises: none of them. Ask an agent to read the code with that exact question. The one habit that works with all three: before trusting a map, ask it three questions you already know the answers to. It takes two minutes and tells you which parts were traced and which were remembered. Both write-ups above are on worklore as stories your agent can redo: what I tried, what failed, the exact steps, and how to check it worked. If you run either one on your own repo, the story page shows whether it worked for other people too.

title: I tried running Sentinel-IR-MCP 0.4+ on my phone via Termux. It stopped me.
author: jackymenCZ (jackymenCZ)
summary: I Tried Running Sentinel-IR-MCP inside Termux on Android. Here is What Happened. Everyone is talking about the new Sentinel-IR-MCP 0.4 release and how it shields your local environment from rogue AI prompts. I don't currently have a PC nearby, so I thought: Why not stretch its limits and test it directly on my smartphone using Termux? I fired up the terminal and ran the setup command: bash npx -y sentinel-ir-mcp@0.4 setup The interactive menu popped up instantly, asking me to choose my AI client: text Connect Sentinel-IR to which client? [1-5] 4 I pressed 4 for VS Code—and Sentinel immediately slapped my wrist with this beautiful security rejection: text sentinel-ir-mcp setup: Refusing to give the agent access to your whole home folder (/data/data/com.termux/files/home). Pass a project folder with --project. ~ $ Why this is brilliant Instead of blindly writing a configuration file and exposing my entire Termux home directory to the AI agent, Sentinel's built-in self-defense instinct kicked in. It detected that my current working directory was the root user folder, recognized the massive security risk (exposing history, config keys, and sensitive data), and pulled the emergency brake instantly. It completely locked out the AI agent before it even had a chance to touch anything. The tool proves that you don't need a bulky PC setup to test zero-trust AI architectures—and its security guard rails are as solid on a mobile terminal as they are in production. title: osFoundry का Agent team क्या करता है, और कब एक ही agent काफ़ी है?
author: tauchiii
summary: मंगलवार सुबह के 7:40 बजे हैं और प्रिया के पास एक सवाल है जिसका जवाब उसकी डायरेक्टर को लंच तक चाहिए: क्या चार दिन का वर्क वीक सच में आउटपुट बनाए रखता है? वह इसे किसी chatbot में पेस्ट करके पूरे भरोसे से लिखा एक पैराग्राफ़ पा सकती है। लेकिन जो model आंकड़े ढूंढेगा, वही यह भी तय करेगा कि आंकड़े सही हैं या नहीं, और वह शायद ही कभी खुद से असहमत होता है। प्रिया चाहती है कि एक व्यक्ति trials ढूंढे, दूसरा आंकड़े निकाले, और कोई तीसरा हर उस चीज़ को वापस भेज दे जिसका कोई source न हो। एक ही स्क्रीन के दो रास्ते osFoundry एक desktop app है जिससे आप AI का काम अपनी ही मशीन पर चला सकते हैं, और इसमें agents को काम सौंपने के दो मिलते-जुलते तरीके हैं। Agent (sidebar में Single agent के नाम से दिखता है) एक नाम वाला agent है जिसका एक ही काम होता है: आप उसे instructions देते हैं, उसे AG-0001L जैसी अपनी ID मिलती है, और उसका हर run रिकॉर्ड होता है ताकि आप बाद में उसे देख सकें। Agent team में specialist members की एक टीम के आगे एक leader होता है। Leader काम की योजना बनाता है, हर step किसी member को देता है, और आप तक पहुंचने से पहले एक reviewer हर step जांचता है। दोनों sidebar में Agents के नीचे एक-दूसरे के बगल में हैं और एक ही स्क्रीन खोलते हैं। फ़र्क़ बस टीम के साइज़ का है। अगर आप कभी ऐसे group chat में रहे हैं जिसमें कोई project manager हो, तो Agent team जाना-पहचाना लगेगा। फ़र्क़ यह है कि हर message, हर handoff और हर फ़ैसला सेव रहता है, और आप scroll करके पीछे देख सकते हैं। टीम स्क्रीन पर एक नज़र यह एक पूरा हो चुका team session है। सवाल और जवाब एक demo run का उदाहरण डेटा हैं। Leader से बातचीत (बीच में)। Header में लिखा है "Leader · Orchestrate your team"। यहीं आप सवाल एक बार पूछते हैं और यहीं मिला-जुला जवाब आता है, यहां एक table के रूप में जिसकी हर row में source है, साथ में एक "Where sources disagree" लाइन और एक "Not covered" लाइन। Session tabs (बीच के ऊपर)। Chat, Team mail, Email, Handoffs, Sub-agents, Proposals और Files। Handoffs दिखाता है कि किसने किसे काम सौंपा। Proposals में वे बदलाव होते हैं जो agents files या settings में सुझाते हैं। कोई सुझाव तब तक लागू नहीं होता जब तक उसे accept न किया जाए। Agent session panel (दाईं ओर)। हर member का एक card है, जिसमें लिखा है कि leader ने उससे क्या करने को कहा, उसने कौन से tools बुलाए ( web_fetch , web_search ) और उसका नतीजा क्या रहा। हर नतीजे के नीचे reviewer का फ़ैसला दिखता है, जैसे "Approved"। ऊपर एक run selector ("Run 1 · 07:40 AM") और Cards / Graph switch है। Team roster tab। यह उन लोगों की लिस्ट है जिन्हें इस session में काम करने की अनुमति है। टीम एक roster है, workflow नहीं। काम का क्रम leader की योजना से तय होता है। Session rail (बाईं ओर, यहां छुपा हुआ) और inspector। Rail में हर session उसकी ID के साथ दिखता है। Inspector में Goal, Trigger और Hooks tabs हैं: finish line के लिए, run किसने शुरू किया उसके लिए, और काम के आसपास के checks के लिए। लोग इसे तीन तरह से इस्तेमाल करते हैं एक researcher जिसे हर आंकड़े का source चाहिए प्रिया Agent team खोलती है और New session दबाती है। New team session dialog में वह "Start from a team" चुना रहने देती है और Team लिस्ट से Deep Research Team चुनती है। Dialog इसके पांच members लोड करता है (deep-research-agent, research-analyst, data-researcher, search-specialist, academic-researcher)। "Who leads" के नीचे Orchestrator दिखता है, जो "plans the work up front, then delegates the steps to the agents below"। वह किसी भी member पर "make leader" दबाकर उसे leader बना सकती है। वह Create दबाती है, leader की chat में अपना सवाल टाइप करती है और भेज देती है। Leader इसे पांच हिस्सों में बांटता है: trials ढूंढना, studies, आंकड़े, उलटे सबूत, और फिर एक जवाब। तीन members एक साथ काम शुरू करते हैं। Data Researcher आंकड़े निकालने से पहले Search Specialist की लिस्ट का इंतज़ार करता है। जब Data Researcher 40% का आंकड़ा रिपोर्ट करता है, तो reviewer उसे "Sent back" मार्क कर देता है, क्योंकि उसमें न source है, न तारीख़, न मापने का पैमाना। वह step दोबारा चलता है, source ढूंढता है, और approve हो जाता है। आख़िर में उसके पास बीच वाले pane में एक जवाब होता है, और उसके हर आंकड़े की जांच उस agent के अलावा किसी और ने की है जिसने उसे ढूंढा था। साथ में एक ईमानदार "Not covered" लाइन भी मिलती है, जिसे वह डायरेक्टर के लिए अपने नोट में पेस्ट कर सकती है। एक solo developer जो बार-बार वही instructions पेस्ट करता है टॉम हफ़्ते में कई बार meeting notes से action items बनाता है, और हर बार पहले नियमों वाला वही पैराग्राफ़ chat में पेस्ट करता है। इस काम के लिए टीम की ज़रूरत नहीं है। ज़रूरत है एक ऐसे agent की जो नियम याद रखे। वह Single agent खोलता है, New session दबाता है और Create in chat tab पर ही रहता है। "New agent" बॉक्स में वह एक लाइन में लिखता है कि उसे क्या चाहिए और Start दबाता है। जो chat खुलती है वह एक setup agent है। वह कुछ सवाल पूछता है, फिर एक नाम, एक @handle और पूरे instructions सुझाता है। Composer के ऊपर एक card आता है जिसमें नाम, handle, Show instructions लिंक और Create agent बटन होता है। वह instructions खोलकर देखता है कि उसका सबसे ज़रूरी नियम उनमें है या नहीं: owner या deadline का कभी अंदाज़ा न लगाना। फिर वह Create agent दबाता है। वही chat अब वह agent बन जाती है। जब वह अपने notes पेस्ट करता है, तो जो owners और तारीख़ें नहीं हैं वे missing मार्क होती हैं, उनका अंदाज़ा कभी नहीं लगाया जाता। Session अपनी Agent ID rail में रखता है, और अगली बार उसे बस agent चुनना होता है। एक release lead जो देखना चाहती है कि किसने क्या किया दारी एक छोटी product team की releases संभालती है। उसके team session में एक leader और Release Drafter, Change Auditor, Docs Reviewer, QA Summarizer और Approval Prep नाम के members हैं। हर एक release package का एक हिस्सा संभालता है। Run से पहले वह Goal tab खोलती है और Set a goal दबाती है। Panel बताता है कि goal को success criteria में बांटा जाता है, जो शुरू में fail रहते हैं और जैसे-जैसे agents उन्हें पूरा करते हैं, हरे हो जाते हैं। Session तब तक चलता रहता है जब तक सब pass न हो जाएं या round limit न आ जाए। वह तीन criteria लिखती है, जिनमें आख़िरी यह है कि approval packet पूरा हो। Members के काम करते समय वह Handoffs देखती है ताकि leader से हर member तक और वापस की chain फ़ॉलो कर सके। वह Proposals भी देखती है कि किसी member ने कोई config बदलाव तो नहीं सुझाया, और वहां कुछ भी उसके बिना लागू नहीं होता। वह किसी भी समय leader की chat में जवाब देकर उसे दिशा दे सकती है, और panel header में Pause दबाकर review करते समय run रोक सकती है। आख़िर में उसके पास release package और यह रिकॉर्ड होता है कि हर हिस्सा किसने draft, audit और approve किया। जो भी पूछे कि notes में कोई लाइन कैसे आई, उसे वह यह दिखा सकती है। बाक़ी app में यह कहां ले जाता है Agent और Agent team वह जगह है जहां काम शुरू होता है। Sessions वह जगह है जहां आप उसे देखते हैं। वह board हर chat, agent, team और terminal session को एक card के रूप में दिखाता है, जो Running, Needs you, Paused, Idle, Done और Failed में इस हिसाब से बंटे होते हैं कि session असल में क्या कर रहा है। जब एक ही team job बार-बार चलानी हो, तो Loop एक roster को trigger, limits और हर round के रिकॉर्ड के साथ लपेट देता है कि कौन से criteria pass हुए। Graphs उस काम के लिए हैं जिसका रास्ता इस पर निर्भर करता है कि बीच में क्या होता है। Leader वाली बातचीत एक Maestro chat है, इसलिए टीम का जवाब आपके बाक़ी Maestro काम में आगे बढ़ सकता है। Session का Enable sync लिंक उसे project के message channel से जोड़ता है, जहां लोग और agents एक ही जगह बात कर सकते हैं। ज़्यादा जानकारी के लिए Agents feature page और agent sessions overview देखें। नए लोग जो सवाल पूछते हैं टीम की जगह single agent कब इस्तेमाल करूं? Single agent तब इस्तेमाल करें जब काम एक साफ़ task हो और नियम तय हों, जैसे notes को reformat करना या एक ही अंदाज़ में जवाब draft करना। टीम तब इस्तेमाल करें जब काम के हिस्सों को अलग-अलग tools चाहिए, या जब आप चाहते हैं कि आपके देखने से पहले कोई अलग reviewer काम जांचे। क्या session शुरू होने के बाद टीम बदल सकते हैं? नहीं। New team session dialog में लिखा है कि टीम "is fixed for this session's life"। Create दबाने से पहले dialog के अंदर आप agents जोड़ या हटा सकते हैं और चुन सकते हैं कि leader कौन होगा। अलग roster के लिए नया session शुरू करें। क्या इसमें से कुछ cloud पर चलता है? New session form में Local और Isolated runs के विकल्प हैं। उसमें लिखा है कि दोनों आपकी मशीन पर आपकी अपनी keys से चलते हैं और कुछ भी cloud पर नहीं जाता। Chat history default रूप से local रहती है। क्या agents अपने instructions खुद बदल सकते हैं? वे बदलाव सुझा सकते हैं, जो Proposals में दिखते हैं। Proposal का मतलब accept हो चुकी configuration नहीं है। Agents अपने prompts छू सकते हैं या नहीं, यह एक अलग setting है। Desktop app आप osfoundry.io/hi/download से ले सकते हैं।

title: Was macht Maestro in osFoundry, ein KI-Chat, der jeden seiner Schritte zeigt?
author: tauchiii
summary: Donnerstag, 4:40 Uhr, und Priya hat einen KI-Assistenten gebeten, auf der Einstellungsseite ihrer App einen Button "Konto löschen" einzubauen. Die Antwort lautet "Erledigt, 4 Dateien geändert." Bevor sie das ausliefert, will sie wissen, welche vier Dateien das sind, was der Assistent gelesen hat, um das zu entscheiden, und ob er dem Billing-Code nahegekommen ist. Ein normales Chatfenster liefert ihr nur den letzten Absatz. Maestro in einem Absatz Maestro ist der KI-Arbeitsbereich mit vollem Werkzeugkasten in der Desktop-App von osFoundry . Du tippst deine Anfrage wie in jedem Chat, aber die Antwort kommt mit ihrem Arbeitsweg: jede aufgelistete Datei, jede ausgeführte Suche, jede gelesene oder bearbeitete Datei und jeder Terminal-Befehl, jeweils als eigene Zeile mit einer Dauer, die du aufklappen kannst. Maestro kann in einem Ordner auf deinem Rechner arbeiten, Änderungen vorschlagen statt sie stillschweigend zu schreiben, und anhalten, um dir einen Plan zu zeigen, bevor es irgendetwas anfasst. Du findest es unter Maestro in der Seitenleiste. Wer ChatGPT oder Claude im Browser kennt: dieselbe Unterhaltung, nur mit dem Aktivitätsprotokoll des Agenten und ein paar Bremsen daneben. Ein Rundgang über den Bildschirm Oben die Bereichs-Tabs. Maestro, Model chat, Multi chat, Research, Wiki und Code liegen alle auf diesem einen Bildschirm. Maestro ist der Tab mit dem kompletten Toolset. Über der Unterhaltung die Detail-Tabs: Chat, Sources, Files, Changelog, Tools, Pipeline und Logs. Das sind verschiedene Ansichten desselben Laufs. Sources hält fest, worauf die Antwort beruht, Changelog listet die Dateien, die dieser Chat geschrieben hat, und Logs zeigt die Schritte und unter Costs, was jede Anfrage gekostet hat. Die Prozesszeilen im Verlauf. Hier hat Maestro src/ aufgelistet (38 Dateien), nach deleteUser gegrept, 0 Treffer gefunden und dann account.ts und users.ts gelesen. Ein Klick auf eine Zeile klappt sie auf und zeigt die genaue Ein- und Ausgabe dieses Tool-Aufrufs. Die Steuerleiste über dem Eingabefeld: Sandbox-Schalter, Plan OFF/ON, Tools und Goal. Unter dem Feld sitzen die Auswahlmenüs für Ordner, Projekt, Repo, Router und Modell. Rechts das Vorschau-Panel, in dem eine Datei, ein Diff oder eine Webseite neben der Unterhaltung aufgeht, statt sie zu ersetzen (Open File / App / Page, Browse Files, Browser). Drei typische Einsatzfälle Eine Solo-Entwicklerin, die den Plan vor der Änderung sehen will Priyas Fall vom Anfang. Die Änderung betrifft Konten und Sessions, also liest sie lieber den Plan, als einen Überraschungs-Diff zu reviewen. Sie klickt in der Steuerleiste auf Plan, sodass dort Plan ON steht. Sie tippt "Add a Delete account button to settings" und schickt es ab. Maestro liest sechs Dateien und ändert keine. Solange der Plan-Modus an ist, verweigert die Desktop-App selbst jedes Tool, das eine Datei schreiben oder einen Befehl ausführen würde. "Nur lesen" ist also keine höfliche Bitte im Prompt. Eine Plan-Karte erscheint mit dem Status "Awaiting approval" und den Buttons Approve und Cancel. Der Plan im Beispiel nennt vier Dateien, sagt, dass src/billing/ unangetastet bleibt, weil Stripe eigene Datensätze führt, und endet mit "Nothing has been changed yet." Sobald der Plan da ist, schaltet sich der Plan-Modus von selbst ab. Priya klickt auf Approve, und erst dann bearbeitet Maestro die vier Dateien und lässt die Tests laufen ( npm test -- account , 3 passed), alles sichtbar als EDIT- und TERMINAL-Zeilen. Hätte ihr der Plan nicht gefallen, hätte Cancel den Ordner exakt so gelassen, wie er war. Was sie am Ende hat: eine Änderung, der sie vorher zugestimmt hat, und einen Verlauf, der zeigt, wo der Agent nachgesehen und was er ausgeführt hat. Ein neuer Kollege, der sich in einer Codebasis zurechtfinden muss Dan ist seit Montag im Team. Er muss herausfinden, wo die Login-Sperre steckt, aber im Code nennt sie niemand "lockout", also findet eine Textsuche nichts. Unter Indexes fügt er den Projektordner einmalig hinzu, damit er sich nach Bedeutung durchsuchen lässt. In einem Maestro-Chat auf diesem Ordner fragt er, wo die App Leute nach fehlgeschlagenen Logins aussperrt. Er verfolgt die Prozesszeilen: eine Ordnersuche mit 2 Ergebnissen, danach ein READ von throttle.ts . Die Antwort verweist auf src/auth/throttle.ts (Zeilen 1–46) und src/routes/session.ts (Zeilen 22–61) und erklärt, dass der Code nie "lock out" sagt: Nach fünf Fehlversuchen setzt er eine Sperrfrist von 15 Minuten und gibt 429 zurück, noch bevor das Passwort geprüft wird. Weil die Antwort Dateipfade enthält und die Zeilen zeigen, was gelesen wurde, kann Dan genau diese Stellen im Vorschau-Panel öffnen und die Aussage selbst prüfen, statt einer Zusammenfassung zu vertrauen. In diesem Fall wird nichts auf die Platte geschrieben, also kann er Approval Mode auf dem Standard lassen. Was er am Ende hat: die zwei Dateien, auf die es ankommt, den Grund, warum die Stichwortsuche sie verfehlt hat, und einen Chat, zu dem er über die Chatliste zurückkehren kann. Eine Marketerin, die Texte in einem fremden Repo bearbeitet Sammy schreibt die Texte für die Launch-Seite, aber die Seite ist eine React-Datei im Engineering-Repo. Der neue Text soll zum Tone-Guide in docs/ passen, und committet werden soll nichts, ohne dass sie draufgeschaut hat. Sie öffnet im Composer das Menü Approval Mode und wählt Permission & Approve, das vor Tool-Aufrufen nachfragt. Die anderen Optionen sind Auto Accept (Standard, Tools laufen sofort), Plan First (erst planen, dann ausführen) und Bypass (gar keine Freigaben, auch nicht für Push und Formularversand). Sie schaltet die Sandbox ein, damit Schreibvorgänge auf einem Branch landen statt im Arbeitsordner. Sie bittet Maestro, die Launch-Seite zu entwerfen und dabei konsistent mit den Docs zu bleiben. Maestro liest docs/tone.md , durchsucht den Code und schlägt eine Änderung an src/Launch.tsx vor. Der Diff öffnet sich im Vorschau-Panel. Sie übernimmt ihn und nutzt dann Export to branch, damit jemand aus dem Engineering ihn wie jede andere Änderung reviewen kann. Was sie am Ende hat: Text, der den befolgten Tone-Guide zitiert (der Sources-Tab hebt ihn auf), einen geprüften Diff und einen Branch statt einer Überraschung auf main. Wo Maestro neben Model chat, Chat und Multi chat steht Maestro teilt sich den Bildschirm mit einfacheren Geschwistern, und wer das richtige wählt, spart Zeit und Geld. Model chat ist ein Tab auf demselben Bildschirm, der jede Runde an ein einzelnes Modell deiner Wahl schickt. Eine reine Lese-Unterhaltung: kein Ordner, keine handelnden Tools, keine Freigaben. Gut für eine schnelle Frage. Chat hat einen eigenen Platz in der Seitenleiste. Auch hier antwortet ein Modell, das du für die ganze Unterhaltung festlegst, aber die Datei-Funktionen bleiben erhalten. Chat kann also eine Änderung vorschlagen, die du mit Accept oder Reject annimmst oder ablehnst, abgelegt unter Changelog. Nimm es, wenn ein bestimmtes Modell die Arbeit machen soll, ohne dass ein Router für dich wählt. Multi chat stellt mehreren Modellen gleichzeitig dieselbe Frage. In Compare liest du die Antworten nebeneinander; in Council antworten die Modelle, bewerten blind die Antworten der anderen, und ein Modell schreibt eine Synthese. Von Maestro aus wandert die Arbeit oft in andere Teile der App. Research macht aus einer Frage einen Bericht mit Quellen, Code lässt einen Coding-Agenten auf eigenem Branch laufen, Indexes macht einen Ordner nach Bedeutung durchsuchbar (wie in Dans Fall), und unter Version → Merge Station werden Sandbox-Änderungen gemergt. Geht eine Runde schief, stellt /rewind im Chat die Dateien wieder her, die diese Runde geändert hat. Wer tiefer einsteigen will: Die Seite zur Maestro-Orchestrierung geht die Detail-Tabs durch, und die Seite zum Plan-Modus erklärt den Freigabeablauf. Die ersten Fragen, die Leute stellen Ist der Plan-Modus nur eine Anweisung im Prompt? Nein. Solange Plan auf ON steht, wird jedes Tool, das nicht auf der Nur-Lese-Liste steht, beim Dispatch durch die App abgewiesen. Der Agent kann also lesen, suchen und browsen, aber nichts bearbeiten und keine Befehle ausführen, bis du den Plan freigibst. Was ist der Unterschied zwischen dem Plan-Schalter und Plan First in Approval Mode? Plan ist ein einmaliger Schalter für die nächste Anfrage: untersuchen, Plan vorlegen, warten. Approval Mode ist die dauerhafte Regel des Chats für Tool-Aufrufe, von Auto Accept bis Bypass. Plan First ist eine ihrer vier Einstellungen. Die vielen Prozesszeilen sind mir zu viel. Kann ich sie ausblenden? Ja. Die Einstellung Process Detail wechselt zwischen Full und Compact. Sie ändert nur die Darstellung der Schritte, nicht den Ablauf der Runde. Welches Modell nutzt Maestro? Standardmäßig wählt der Router pro Runde ein Modell, und die Prozesszeilen zeigen, welches gelaufen ist. Den Modellmodus (Cloud, lokal oder selbst gehostet) stellst du im Composer um, oder du nimmst Chat, wenn ein Modell für die ganze Unterhaltung fest bleiben soll. Die Desktop-App gibt es unter osfoundry.io/de/download .
